query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of aluminum to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, stable Al2O3 tribofilm that maintains low friction and wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a solid solution microstructure that shows low friction at room temperature but increased friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to deleterious tribochemical reactions.
generation.intervention: A minor alloying addition (e.g., 3–5 atomic % Al) into the CoCrFeNi matrix.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests in ambient air under dry conditions, with typical loads around 1 N, sliding speeds near 0.1 m/s, and a temperature range spanning from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The controlled formation of a nanocrystalline, adherent Al2O3 (alumina) layer acting as a tribofilm that provides lubrication at low temperatures and thermal/chemical protection at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the minor Al content enables the formation of a thin, lubricious alumina layer that reduces metal-to-metal contact. At elevated temperatures (up to 800 °C), the high thermal stability of Al2O3 leads to a protective oxide scale that minimizes further tribochemical oxidation and abrasive wear, thereby maintaining low friction and wear rates across the entire test regime.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the Al-doped alloy is expected to exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy maintains low friction at room temperature but suffers from increased friction and higher wear rates at elevated temperatures due to uncontrolled oxidations and tribochemical reactions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable under dry sliding conditions in ambient air, with sliding loads around 1 N and speeds approximately 0.1 m/s, across temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: While the protective role of Al2O3 is well-documented at high temperatures, the exact balance between improved tribological performance and any possible negative effects (e.g., phase stability or ductility alterations) at lower temperatures remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets: one of standard CoCrFeNi alloy and another of CoCrFeNi alloy with a 3–5 at.% Al addition. Under identical dry sliding test conditions (load ~1 N, speed ~0.1 m/s) perform experiments at room temperature and at 800 °C. Characterize the worn surfaces and tribofilms using XRD, TEM, and surface profilometry.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per unit distance and load)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in both coefficient of friction and wear rate at both room temperature and 800 °C relative to the baseline, or if undesired deleterious phases emerge that compromise mechanical integrity, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
